title: To keep drug prices high, pharma has been piling up the patents
gist: A JAMA study led by S. Sean Tu found patents per FDA-approved small-molecule drug tripled from 2.1 in 1990 to 6.9 in 2019, driven by nonprimary 'patent thicket' patents, extending patented time from 2 to 6.1 years; authors call for USPTO scrutiny, limits on add-on patents and disgorgement remedies.

insights.claim: The average number of patents per approved small-molecule drug more than tripled from 2.1 in 1990 to 6.9 in 2019.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Patent stacking is a key lever pharma uses to extend brand exclusivity and revenue.
insights.quote: going from an average of 2.1 patents per drug approved in 1990 to 6.9 for those approved in 2019
insights.locator: A study published Monday in JAMA

insights.claim: Increasing patents per drug extended the average patented period from two years in 1990 to 6.1 years in 2019.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Longer exclusivity delays generic erosion, supporting branded drug revenues.
insights.locator: The study—led by S. Sean Tu

insights.claim: Of 10,940 patents on 1,981 small-molecule drugs approved by the FDA from 1990 to 2019, 84% were nonprimary patents covering things like inactive ingredients, usage changes or delivery devices, while primary patents changed little.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Exclusivity is increasingly built on minor modifications rather than new therapeutic innovation.

insights.claim: Patent thickets of nonprimary patents delay affordable generics and keep drug prices high without clinical advancement.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Generic manufacturers face longer delays; branded pharma benefits from prolonged pricing power.
insights.locator: Most of the growth was in “nonprimary” patents

insights.claim: The study likely underestimates current thickets because patent activity now extends up to nine years after FDA approval.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Exclusivity extension may be even larger for recent drugs.
insights.locator: For the study, Tu and colleagues

insights.claim: Per capita inflation-adjusted US prescription drug spending rose from $291 in 1990 to $1,084 in 2019, per Peterson-KFF, and Americans spend nearly twice the average of other high-income countries, per the Commonwealth Fund.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: High US drug spending sustains political pressure for pricing and patent reform.

insights.claim: Drugmakers argue extra patents don't delay generics, but their examples are often pre-2010 drugs approved when thickets were smaller; the study itself did not directly measure generic delays.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Industry defenses may weaken as evidence on post-2010 thickets accumulates.
insights.locator: A key limitation of the study

insights.claim: The authors call for more USPTO scrutiny, laws limiting minor add-on patents, and court-ordered disgorgement for patent abuse, warning that without reform exclusivity will be disconnected from innovation.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Patent reform could shorten exclusivity periods and hit branded pharma revenue tails.
insights.quote: will likely entrench extended exclusivity periods that are disconnected from meaningful therapeutic innovation and continue to complicate and delay generic entry
